guide.title: East Harlem, Manhattan: Italian Harlem to El Barrio
guide.intro: East Harlem stayed largely rural until an elevated line reached it in 1879-1880 and the Lexington Avenue subway followed in 1918, opening the land to development. Southern Italian and Sicilian immigrants arrived from the 1870s on, and by the 1930s more than 110,000 Italian Americans lived here as Italian Harlem, a community whose remnants survive around Pleasant Avenue and institutions like Patsy's Pizzeria, which opened in 1933, and Rao's. After World War I, Puerto Rican and Latin American migrants built an enclave around 110th Street and Lexington Avenue; the Puerto Rican population reached about 63,000 by 1950, and the neighborhood became known as Spanish Harlem and, to residents, El Barrio. La Marqueta, the market beneath the Park Avenue railroad viaduct, was officially sanctioned by the city in 1936 and held over 500 vendors at its 1950s-60s peak. El Museo del Barrio, a community museum of Puerto Rican, Latin American, and Caribbean art, was founded here in 1969.

sections.heading: Italian Harlem to El Barrio
sections.body: East Harlem's two great immigrant chapters left their mark on the same blocks. Italian workers arrived from the 1870s, and Italian Harlem peaked in the 1930s with more than 110,000 Italian Americans, remembered today around Pleasant Avenue and the Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, and in Patsy's Pizzeria (1933) and Rao's, founded 1896. After World War I, Puerto Rican and Latin American migrants settled around 110th Street and Lexington Avenue; by 1950 the Puerto Rican population had reached about 63,000, and the neighborhood became known as Spanish Harlem and, to residents, El Barrio, later noted for its contributions to salsa and Latin freestyle music. La Marqueta, sanctioned by the city in 1936 beneath the Park Avenue viaduct, held over 500 vendors at its 1950s-60s peak as a central social and economic hub for Hispanic New York; in 2026 the city announced plans for a city-owned grocery store on the site. El Museo del Barrio, founded in 1969 by artist-educator Rafael Montañez Ortíz as a community alternative to orthodox museums, remains devoted to Puerto Rican, Latin American, and Caribbean art.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: East Harlem is served chiefly by the IRT Lexington Avenue line — 6 local trains at 96th, 103rd, 110th, and 116th Streets and the 4/5/6 express hub at 125th Street-Lexington Avenue — plus the Q at 96th Street/Second Avenue on the neighborhood's southern edge and Metro-North commuter trains at Harlem-125th Street. Second Avenue Subway Phase 2, under construction since 2024 with major tunneling beginning in June 2026, will eventually extend the Q to 106th, 116th, and 125th Streets, but those stations are not yet open.

faq.question: How do I get to East Harlem by subway?
faq.answer: Take the 6 local to 96th, 103rd, 110th, or 116th Streets, or the 4/5/6 express to 125th Street-Lexington Avenue. The Q reaches the neighborhood's southern edge at 96th Street/Second Avenue, and Metro-North stops at Harlem-125th Street.

faq.question: What is La Marqueta?
faq.answer: A public market beneath the Park Avenue railroad viaduct between East 111th and 116th Streets, officially sanctioned by the city in 1936 and once home to more than 500 vendors at its 1950s-60s peak; it remains an active city property today.

faq.question: Why is East Harlem also called Spanish Harlem or El Barrio?
faq.answer: Puerto Rican and Latin American migrants settled around 110th Street and Lexington Avenue after World War I; by 1950 the Puerto Rican population had reached about 63,000, and the community became known as Spanish Harlem and, to residents, El Barrio.

faq.question: Is Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 open yet?
faq.answer: No. Major tunneling began in June 2026 on the roughly 1.5-mile, $6 billion extension that will bring the Q to 106th, 116th, and 125th Streets, but none of those East Harlem stations are open to riders yet.

faq.question: Where can I stay in East Harlem?
faq.answer: No hotel or bed-and-breakfast within East Harlem itself could be verified as operating. Travelers typically stay in Central Harlem or on the Upper East Side, both a short ride away on the 4/5/6 or Q.

places.name: El Museo del Barrio
places.address: 1230 Fifth Avenue (at 104th Street), New York, NY
places.summary: Founded in 1969 by Rafael Montañez Ortíz as a museum for the Puerto Rican community of El Barrio; holds 6,500-plus works spanning 800-plus years of Latin American and Caribbean art; its Teatro reopened in 2021 after restoration.

places.name: Museum of the City of New York
places.address: 1220 Fifth Avenue at 103rd Street, New York, NY
places.summary: City-history museum at the neighborhood's southwest corner; 2026 exhibitions include 'Another Wonderland,' a restored New Deal-era children's-hospital mural cycle, and 'He Built This City,' a handmade architectural model of New York. Open every day.

places.name: Thomas Jefferson Park
places.address: First Avenue and FDR Drive, between E 111th and E 114th Streets, Manhattan
places.summary: Neighborhood park with a running track, baseball and handball courts, a recreation center, and a seasonal outdoor pool; received expansion planning in the mid-1930s under Mayor La Guardia.

places.name: La Marqueta
places.address: Park Avenue beneath the Metro-North viaduct, between E 111th and E 116th Streets, Manhattan
places.summary: Historic public market officially sanctioned by the city in 1936, once home to more than 500 vendors at its 1950s-60s peak; today hosts a small group of food vendors and the HBK Incubates kitchen-incubator. In 2026 the city announced a city-owned grocery store planned for the site.

places.name: Rao's
places.summary: A restaurant established in 1896. Wikipedia names the founder as Joshua Anthony Rao, who ran it until his death in 1909; the restaurant's own site names Charles Rao. Wikipedia quotes the New York Post calling it 'one of the hardest places to get into in the city.'
places.history: Vincent and Louis Rao took the restaurant on after their father's death in 1909. Patrons named by Wikipedia include John Gotti, Rudy Giuliani, Robert De Niro and Bo Dietl, with Woody Allen and Mia Farrow regulars in the 1980s. A spinoff at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas opened in 2006 and closed in 2021; a Hollywood spinoff opened in 2013 and closed on February 28, 2026; a Miami Beach location opened at a Loews hotel in 2023. The Rao's brand also sells packaged sauces, pasta, soups and frozen meals, and is owned by The Campbell's Company.

places.name: Patsy's Pizzeria
places.address: 2287 First Avenue (at E 118th Street), New York, NY
places.summary: A pizzeria that opened in 1933 in Italian Harlem, founded by Pasquale 'Patsy' Lancieri at 2287 First Avenue near East 117th Street. Lancieri is said to have learned his craft at Lombardi's coal oven, and the business claims to have originated selling pizza by the slice.
places.history: Lancieri died in the 1970s, and in 1991 his widow sold the pizzeria to Frank Brija, an Albanian immigrant from Kosovo, who trademarked the name and expanded it to more than twelve locations in New York. In 2019 a waiter returned a customer's lost cashier's check for $423,987.55. The pizzeria appeared on the Cooking Channel's 'Man v. Food' in 2020, and in 2024 its storefront facade was recreated as a film set in England for 'A Quiet Place: Day One.'

places.name: Ollin (Cafe Ollin)
places.summary: Family-run Mexican restaurant serving chorizo burritos, cemitas, and a bottomless brunch.

places.name: La Fonda (La Fonda Boricua)
places.summary: Puerto Rican establishment of 35-plus years on the 106th Street cultural corridor, known for home-style cooking with live Latin jazz.

places.name: Super Nice Coffee and Bakery
places.summary: Neighborhood takeout-window coffee shop and bakery selling specialty donuts such as glazed loganberry.
